title: Almost-linear-work parallel exact maximum flow
formal: For every fixed integer \(a\ge1\), is there a uniform bounded-error randomized parallel algorithm that computes an exact maximum flow in any directed graph with integer capacities in \(\{0,\ldots,n^{a}\}\), using \((m+n)^{1+o(1)}\) work and \((m+n)^{o(1)}\) depth?
definitions: The graph is given by its vertex set \([n]=\{1,\ldots,n\}\), with \(n\ge2\), and an explicit list of \(m\) arcs. It has no loops and at most one arc per ordered pair; opposite arcs are allowed. A feasible flow assigns a value \(f_{e}\) to every arc with \(0\le f_{e}\le u_{e}\) and equal incoming and outgoing total flow at each vertex except the distinct specified source \(s\) and sink \(t\). Its value is outgoing minus incoming flow at \(s\). The required output is a feasible flow attaining the largest possible value, including every arc value. Output integral arc flows. Use a synchronous priority CRCW PRAM: concurrent reads are allowed; if several processors write one cell in a round, the lowest-index writer succeeds. Each active processor executes one word-RAM instruction per round, with the instructions and word length specified below. Work is the total number of executed processor instructions, including activation, input access and output; depth is the number of rounds. Processor IDs and addresses fit in words. All processors run a fixed finite program with their IDs; there is no advice or free preprocessing. Independent uniform random words cost one instruction each. The entire output is correct with probability at least \(2/3\). Both resource bounds hold on every execution. Use a uniform word RAM with word length \(w=d\lceil\log_{2}(n+2)\rceil\), for a fixed positive integer \(d\) chosen with the algorithm and large enough for its addresses and input values. Unit-cost instructions are word reads/writes, copying, comparisons, branching, Boolean operations, shifts, addition, subtraction and multiplication modulo \(2^{w}\), and integer quotient and remainder with nonzero divisor. Shifts by at least \(w\) return zero. Multiword computation is charged by its component instructions. The fixed finite program receives no advice or precomputed tables; all initialization, preprocessing and output writes count. With \(N=m+n\), require a function \(h_{a}:\mathbb{N}\to[1,\infty)\) satisfying \(\lim_{N\to\infty}\log h_{a}(N)/\log N=0\), such that work is at most \(C_{a}Nh_{a}(N)\) and depth at most \(C_{a}h_{a}(N)\). The program, \(d\), \(C_{a}\) and \(h_{a}\) may depend on \(a\), but not on the graph. Initially the explicit input is in shared memory; all subsequent computation is charged.

context_blocks.text: Sequential almost-linear time does not imply that the same computation can be completed with very few dependent stages. This target asks for both near-optimal total work and subpolynomial parallel depth.

Haeupler, Jiang and Saranurak explicitly identify almost-optimal parallel exact maximum flow as a major open problem. Their DAG Projections paper gives efficient reductions between exact directed flow and approximation problems on directed acyclic graphs.

The reductions classify the difficulty of several parallel tasks; they do not establish the requested work and depth. The capacity restriction makes each numerical input occupy logarithmically many bits.

why: This is a central unresolved parallelization problem for exact network optimization, asking whether near-optimal sequential work can coexist with subpolynomial dependence depth.
answer_criterion: Prove the stated existence claim or its logical negation, with the specified model, quantifiers and guarantees. A conditional lower bound settles only its conditional claim. Benchmark acceptance requires a complete mathematically correct proof checked in Lean; a partial improvement does not meet the target.

sentences: The task is exact maximum flow in a directed graph with polynomially bounded integer capacities.
The question asks for almost-linear total parallel work and subpolynomial depth.
Bounded-error randomization is allowed in a uniform shared-memory parallel model.
Sequential almost-linear algorithms do not provide the requested bound on dependent stages.
DAG projection reductions connect several versions of this open parallel flow problem.
